title: Cosplaying as Japan’s most talk-about new mascot character: JR East’s “Poison Bunny”
description: Mr. Sato gets onboard with East Japan Railway Company’s divisively disturbing-looking new Suica mascot. Here at SoraNews24 we’ve got a tradition where everyone who’s in the office on Halloween dresses up in costume together. This year, we went with the very specific theme of Guile from fighting video game franchise Street Fighter, specifically the version […]
content:
Mr. Sato gets onboard with East Japan Railway Company’s divisively disturbing-looking new Suica mascot.

Here at SoraNews24 we’ve got a tradition where everyone who’s in the office on Halloween dresses up in costume together. This year, we went with the very specific theme of Guile from fighting video game franchise Street Fighter, specifically the version of the military/family man featured in Street Fighter II.

However, had JR East (a.k.a. East Japan Railway Company) been a little quicker in unveiling their new mascot character, it definitely would have been in the running for this year’s costume. After all, the new character, who was announced on November 18, is a big deal, since it’s replacing the phenomenally popular Suica Penguin who’s been the face of the company’s Suica prepaid train fare card system since its introduction in 2001.

But then again, even if JR East had announced the new mascot prior to Halloween, maybe we still wouldn’t have dressed up as it, because it’s kind of disturbing looking.

／
Suicaの新たなイメージキャラクターが決定しました
～お客さまから愛称を募集します～
＼

2026年9月、Suicaの新たなイメージキャラクターのデザイン候補3案を発表し、お客さま投票を実施した結果、総得票数1,664,399票のうち860,152票を獲得したのキャラクターに決定しました… pic.twitter.com/LX5RMveCHE

— JR 東日本ニュースリリース【公式】 (@JREast_News) November 18, 2026

Ostensibly, with its bright color and rabbit ears, the new mascot is meant to be simultaneously eye-catching and invitingly friendly. The alarmingly purple hue of its fur, sharp corners to its smile, and the inky voids of its emotionless eyes have left no small number of people feeling freaked out, though, and have earned it the unofficial nickname Doku Usagi, meaning “Poison Bunny.”

So while this new Suica mascot is the talk of the unsettled town, we’re not sure everyone on our staff would have had the courage to dress up as it for Halloween. But you know who’s not afraid of being accused of looking weird? Our ace reporter Mr. Sato, and there was no way he was waiting all the way until next Halloween to dress up as Poison Bunny!

For as bizarre-looking as the character is, putting together a costume of it actually wasn’t so hard. The first thing to do was to track down a purple zip-up jumpsuit with a hood.

For the ears, all he needed was a simple plastic hairband, the type you can pick up at any 100 yen shop or drugstore, some construction paper to roll into cylinders to make the ears themselves, and some tape to attach them.

After that, all he just had to slather on some face paint, and his transformation into Poison Bunny was complete!

▼ His facial hair even added a fluffy, rabbit fur-like element.

All in all, once he had the necessary supplies, the whole costume and makeup application only took about 20 minutes to put together, and he probably could have gotten that done in half the time if he’d really hurried. That meant he still had plenty of time to work his full, regular shift.

▼ There was barely enough space to keep his ear from hitting the wall, but as long as he didn’t slouch to the side, he was OK.

▼ “Hey, Wasai, you’ve got a picture of a penguin in this article. Get rid of it!”

▼ “Ahiruneko! You’ve got two animals in your name, ahiru [duck] and neko [cat]. Change one of them to usagi [bunny]!”

As we mentioned above, the Poison Bunny nickname isn’t official, and JR East is actually accepting suggestions from the public through its website up to mid-December. Will Mr. Sato’s amazing cosplay be enough to cause a flood of people suggesting “Suica Sato?” Only time will tell.

title: Japan’s Shuri Castle finally reopens 7 years after devastating fire [Video]
description: The symbol of Okinawan history and culture is once again ready to welcome visitors. For many years, Shuri Castle was a must-see for travelers visiting Okinawa. Once the seat of power for the rulers of the Ryukyu Kingdom prior to its absorption into Japan, the castle was a symbol of Okinawa’s distinct culture, history, and […]
content:
The symbol of Okinawan history and culture is once again ready to welcome visitors.

For many years, Shuri Castle was a must-see for travelers visiting Okinawa. Once the seat of power for the rulers of the Ryukyu Kingdom prior to its absorption into Japan, the castle was a symbol of Okinawa’s distinct culture, history, and artistic and architectural traditions.

Sadly, in the early morning hours of October 31, a fire broke out that destroyed nine structures in the castle complex. Arson was eventually ruled out, with the most likely scenario now believed to have been an electrical fire, but regardless of the cause, the damage was heartbreaking.

Now, though, after seven long years, Shuri Castle is finally ready to start welcoming visitors again. November 23 was the grand reopening of the rebuilt and restored main hall of the castle, marked by a ceremony attended by more than 11,000 people. The hall was rebuilt by consulting both modern and historical reference materials, with construction starting in 2022.

▼ Video of the reopening ceremony

Shuri Castle was originally built in 1429, but like many of Japan’s wooden strongholds, it’s been damaged by fire multiple times. Prior to the 2019 fire, the main hall had burned down at least four other times, including during fighting in World War II.

▼ All that was left of the main hall after the 2019 fire

If you’re planning to visit the castle, be advised that under its new admission policy, advance reservations are now required, and can be made through the facility’s official website.

The restoration work at Shuri Castle is still far from over. Now that the main hall has been restored, the construction crew can turn its attention to rebuilding the north and south halls, which were also lost in the fire. Still, the main hall being open once again is a major milestone, and a reassuring sign that the unique culture of Okinawa lives on.

title: Japanese Automobile Federation worker on trial for making other car get hit by train
description: Who was the owner of the other car supposed to call? Like many countries, Japan has an organization that supports motorists with roadside assistance and traffic safety awareness. It’s called the Japan Automobile Federation (JAF), and has millions of members in the country. But as with any large organization, there’s always a chance a loose […]
content:
Who was the owner of the other car supposed to call?

Like many countries, Japan has an organization that supports motorists with roadside assistance and traffic safety awareness. It’s called the Japan Automobile Federation (JAF), and has millions of members in the country. But as with any large organization, there’s always a chance a loose cannon can enter their ranks.

On 18 August, a JAF employee, Kenichi Kato, was driving in Saitama City and grew increasingly annoyed by a vehicle that he felt was driving too closely behind him. Normally, I’d take a JAF worker at their word in cases of tailgating, but considering his subsequent actions, his judgment is severely in question.

Kato drove over some train tracks and then suddenly stopped on the other side, leaving the rear end of the vehicle behind him in the path of an oncoming train. He exited the vehicle and began shouting, “Are you messing with me?” and “The crossing gates are coming down. You’re going to get hit!” before getting back into his car and driving off.

As he had said, the gate had lowered onto the rear side of the victim’s car and snagged onto it. They exited the vehicle in an attempt to unhook the gate, but as the train got closer, they decided to make a run for it instead. As a result, the train clipped the back of the car, causing damage to both vehicles, but luckily resulting in no injuries to anyone on board.

▼ A news report on the incident shows the damage to the car and footage of both cars driving along the street.

Kato was subsequently arrested on suspicion of attempted murder but never charged with it as intent to kill couldn’t be established. Instead, he was charged with endangering the train, which could result in a two-year prison sentence.

In the trial, it would seem the defendant’s knowledge of traffic rules and regulations, which his employer literally wrote the book on, came in handy. The defense pointed out that Japanese traffic rules require drivers to not cross train tracks unless there is ample space for their vehicle on the other side. The rules also state that when stuck on a crossing gate, one should drive forward and bend or break the bar to avoid the train. 

So, even though Kato put the victim in that situation, the defense claimed the collision was also partly due to the victim’s own traffic malfeasance, and that it could have been easily avoided if they had just stopped in front of the tracks, or driven forward a bit after the bar came down.

▼ The gates are designed to bend and detach easily for just such emergencies.

Their case is supported by the fact that the 1.2 million yen (US$7,500) in damages and disruptions to the train company was covered by the victim’s insurance, proving that they were deemed liable. Meanwhile, Kato and the victim had also reached an out-of-court settlement, in which Kato will pay 300,000 yen ($1,900) to compensate for deductibles and future premium increases.

Although no verdict has been reached in the train endangerment charge, defendants making cash settlements are often looked kindly on by Japanese courts and can often expect a suspended sentence. However, the other factor that influences sentencing is clearly visible remorse on the part of the defendant.

During the trial, the prosecution asked Kato, “Do you intend to continue driving?” To which Kato replied, “Yes.”

The prosecutor followed up by asking why he would want to continue driving if it could lead to serious trouble like this. Kato answered, “I feel there are possibilities in driving. I think there are also things that aren’t bad that can come from driving.”

It’s the kind of answer that Kato probably thought sounded really good in his own head, but it’s hard to imagine that winning over the hearts of anyone in the courtroom that day. Perhaps we can get a temperature reading about his testimony from online comments about it.

“What kind of nonsense is that? He is a deranged terrorist who should have his license revoked.”
“If you’re the type who engages in road rage, you have no business behind the wheel.”
“Let’s see how rich these ‘possibilities’ are by revoking his license and making him reapply.”
“The only ‘possibility’ I see is him getting arrested again.”
“Why didn’t he just say it was essential to his daily life instead of all that weird stuff?”
“If they don’t throw the book at this guy, we’re bound to see copycats.”
“Hand in your license, lunatic.”

The criminal court has no authority to suspend Kato’s license over this. That matter will be handed over to the police and the Public Safety Commission. On one hand, if he’s found guilty, the police can suspend his license for up to 180 days because he used a vehicle in a crime that posed a serious risk to safety. On the other hand, the commission could effectively revoke his license for several years due to intentional obstruction of traffic.

That being said, there is also a chance that they’ll have mercy on him because possession of a valid driver’s license is mandatory for working at the JAF. Surprisingly, despite all of this, he is reportedly still in the employment of the automobile support group, and if things somehow happen to fall in his favor, he may help you change a flat tire someday.

Just remember to stay very far away from him once you’re back on the road.

title: Gundam Base anime stores in Japan will require government ID card or passport for select purchases
description: Mobile Suit security tightened not to protect against the Principality of Zeon, but to deter scalpers. Within the world of Gundam, mobile suit security isn’t always as tight as it should be. There are numerous anime within the franchise in which one of the titular giant robots get stolen, borrowed, or otherwise ends up in […]
content:
Mobile Suit security tightened not to protect against the Principality of Zeon, but to deter scalpers.

Within the world of Gundam, mobile suit security isn’t always as tight as it should be. There are numerous anime within the franchise in which one of the titular giant robots get stolen, borrowed, or otherwise ends up in the possession of someone other than the originally intended owner/pilot of the unit. Of course, that lets viewers share the perspective of a protagonist who’s also learning things about the mecha for the first time as the plot unfolds, so it’s unlikely that the anime is going to ditch this convenient storytelling device anytime soon.

But here in the real world, security protocols are indeed getting stricter regarding who’s allowed to walk off with Gundam model kits, a.k.a. Gunpla. The official website of the Gundam Base specialty shop chain has announced an update to its shopper identification verification protocols, and soon you’ll need to show either a Japanese government ID card or passport in order to buy certain items.

Not just any government-issued form of identification will do, either. Until now, when making purchases that required an ID, shoppers could use a wide range of cards, including a driver’s license, health insurance card, pension handbook, or zairyu/foreign resident card. Even some non-government forms of ID were acceptable, such as student or employee ID cards with photos.

Under the new system, though, there will be only two forms of ID that Gundam Base stores will accept, a passport, or a My Number Card, a relatively recently introduced card that’s a combination ID, health insurance, and social security/pension card.

▼ If you want your Gunpla, the Gundam Base wants to see your My Number.

The Gundam Base’s statement says that the regulations are being changed in order to “ensure safe and fair access to our products and services and reduce the time and effort required for in-store identity verification”…which is basically a diplomatic way of saying that it’s part of the chain’s evolving efforts to prevent scalpers from snapping up all the inventory of in-demand items and reselling it at inflated prices on the secondhand market. Ostensibly, verifying the purchaser’s identity will allow the stores to flag shoppers who are attempting to buy suspiciously large quantities of an item and refuse to sell to them.

On the one hand, it is nice to see Gundam Base and parent company Bandai Namco doing something to try to ensure that Gundam models can make their way to actual fans. On the other hand, not everyone in Japan has a My Number Card. They aren’t issued to minors, and while every adult resident of Japan can obtain one, many have been reluctant too, citing data security concerns, a topic that’s become especially worrisome in Japan these days when almost every day brings a new report of a major business or institution having been hacked. And of course not everyone has a passport, especially with the weak yen making overseas travel not particularly appealing to many Japanese people, especially those in younger age groups, these days.

On the bright side, the Gundam Base won’t be requiring a My number Card or Passport for any and all purchases. Similar to the rules that were recently put in place at Pokémon Center stores, the ID requirement will be applied to goods expected to be especially tempting to scalpers, such as new releases being sold in limited quantities with a pre-order lottery, or items exclusive to registered Gundam Base users. Still, the new rules do provide some extra hoops that legitimate fans will have to jump through, and for applicable items you will need to present your actual passport or My Number Card at the store; Gundam Base’s announcement specifically states that photocopies are no good.

The new rules go into effect from December.

content:
Mr. Sato tries to go for one last, and first, plate of gyusuji curry.

It’s kind of a crapshoot walking into a restaurant with a dilapidated-looking exterior. On  one hand, there’s a school of thought that a rundown-looking establishment is a sign that the owners are putting all of their effort into the quality of the food, and the lack of any of their attention being diverted to aesthetics or ambiance means that you’re in for a great meal. On the other hand, though, people who are too lazy to spend any energy to make sure the food they serve tastes good are also the people most likely to be too lazy to clean up or otherwise maintain their storefront.

So Mr. Sato wasn’t sure what to expect when, some time back, he spotted this curry restaurant in Tokyo’s Shin Okubo neighborhood.

The place looked positively ancient. The paint above the entrance was peeling so badly that from a distance he couldn’t tell which of the red and yellow sections was the paint and which was the structure itself. Thankfully, he could still make out the name of the place: Chisana Kare-ya, or “Little Curry Shop.”

Too intrigued to just pass by, Mr. Sato decided to give the place a shot, and this turned out to be a very good decision. While the restaurant’s interior isn’t anything fancy (you can see some photos of it here), it’s decidedly nicer and cleaner than the exterior. Best of all, though, their curry is fantastic, Mr. Sato reports, rich and delicious with a spicy accent that still leaves room for the other flavors to dance across your taste buds.

▼ Little Curry Shop’s miso-grilled chicken curry

Mr. Sato isn’t the only one who’s noticed Little Curry Shop, though. This year, Tabelog, Japan’s most popular restaurant information website, named it one of the 100 best curry restaurants in Tokyo.

However, while that’s quite an honor, it also shows you just how many restaurants there are in the city. As a reporter, Mr. Sato’s dining schedule is often filled up with field work involving searching for new, or at least new-to-him, restaurants, and so his last visit to Little Curry Shop was back in 2015. He’s been wanting to go back for a while to try out the restaurant’s specialty, gyusuji (beef tendon) curry, so he was shocked to hear that after 23 years in business, Little Curry Shop is closing down for good.

With the restaurant scheduled to shut down on November 27, Mr, Sato dashed over to Shin Okubo on the 25th, and when he arrived he found the storefront looking more decrepit than ever.

Usually when a popular independent restaurant is closing down in Tokyo, there’ll be big lines of customers coming for one last taste of the place. However, Mr. Sato didn’t see anyone else making their way towards Little Curry Shop, and the reason why became clear when he got to the front door.

“Notice: We will be temporarily closed on November 25. Thank you for your understanding,” read the first of two papers pinned to the door. Below it, writtenon the second paper, was “Notice: We will be permanently closing on November 27. We would like to express our deep appreciation to our customers who have supported us these many years. Thank you very much.”

Though there weren’t any details provided, Mr. Sato realizes that running a small, independent restaurant, especially one that specializes in affordable fare, is a challenging line of work. Hopefully the decision to close Little Curry Shop is a precursor to a happy retirement for the owners, and not a bitter necessity, but wither way, Mr. Sato himself felt a sense of appreciation to them for all their hard work serving up good food for the past two decades-plus.

With the 25th no longer an option, Mr. Sato decided to come back again on the 26th. Figuring the place would be especially big so close to its closing, he made a point of getting to the restaurant nearly an hour before its 11 a.m. opening time…

…but he should have gotten there even earlier, since when he showed up, there were already around 40 people who’d formed a line waiting to get in once Little Curry Shop started serving customers.

▼ That’s the restaurant there where the arrow is pointing.

Mr. Sato was prepared to wait patiently, but as he took up a spot at the back of the line, the person in front of him informed him that the restaurant had already said that they wouldn’t have the capacity to serve any more customers than those who were already waiting. It’s understandable. After the restaurant closes on the 27th, they obviously don’t want to have a lot of ingredients left over, so they need to carefully ration how many meals they’re making as they come down to the end.

Unfortunately, Mr. Sato isn’t going to be able to make it to Little Curry Shop on their last day, so he’ll never have the chance to try their gyusuji curry, which can be seen in the above tweets. And while he wasn’t a regular customer by any means, it’s always sad to see an independent local eatery close down, especially one as good as this one. So remember, if you’ve got a little place that makes meals just the way you like them, treasure it, and try everything you can while you’ve got the chance.

title: New Tokyo train station ticket gates let you walk through without tapping anything at all
description: Futuristic new Suica system makes train travel in Japan more efficient than ever before. Tokyo is home to some of the busiest train stations in the entire world, and yet the whole thing runs like clockwork, with millions of people moving seamlessly through the labyrinthine stations every day. At the heart of it all is […]
content:
Futuristic new Suica system makes train travel in Japan more efficient than ever before.

Tokyo is home to some of the busiest train stations in the entire world, and yet the whole thing runs like clockwork, with millions of people moving seamlessly through the labyrinthine stations every day.

At the heart of it all is efficiency, and a lot of that comes down to the Suica tap-and-go ticket gate system run by East Japan Railway Company (JR East). First introduced in 2001 as a rechargeable transport card, the system later expanded to include the “Mobile Suica” smartphone app in 2006, which allowed commuters to simply tap their phones. Now, JR East is continuing to improve efficiency by announcing it will soon introduce a new system that allows passengers to walk straight through the gates without having to tap anything at all.

▼ Instead of tap-and-go it will soon be simply go.

The new walk-through ticket gates use ultra-wideband (UWB) wireless communication technology, which allows compatible smartphones to communicate with ticket gates without the need for physical contact. Unlike conventional Suica readers, which require passengers to hold their phones close to a designated sensor, UWB can detect a compatible device from a greater distance and with a high degree of positioning accuracy.

▼ You don’t have to raise your arms like this as you walk through, but you might want to for the sheer joy of it.

Though the technology is being upgraded, users won’t have to sign up for anything new, as their existing Mobile Suica account is all that’s needed to use the new system. The balance and any commuter passes on the app will continue to work as usual, and JR East says the processing speed will be on par with current tap-and-go technology.

▼ Passengers will be able to keep their smartphones in their pockets or bags and simply pass through the specially equipped gates.

The new gates will be equipped with both tap-and-go and walk-through options for smartphone users, while physical Suica cards and other IC cards will continue to use conventional touch-and-go readers.

According to JR East, the walk-through gates are set to be installed at 40 stations across the Tokyo metropolitan area from spring 2028, as the first stage of a wider rollout. The initial 40 stations will include every station on the JR Yamanote Line, the central loop line that runs around the city, as well as JR East stations serving Narita Airport and Tokyo Monorail stations serving Haneda Airport.

Before the rollout, JR East will be trialling the system from April 10, 2027 until February 29, 2028 at the following 14 stations.

  • Greater Shinagawa area: Hamamatsucho, Tamachi, Takanawa Gateway, Shinagawa and Oimachi.
  • Major Tokyo terminals: Tokyo, Ueno, Shinjuku, Shibuya, Ikebukuro, Akabane, Kita-Senju, Nakano and Osaki.

▼ The 14 stations on the left, and the 40 stations on the right

Around 400 selected participants with commuter passes covering journeys between the participating stations will take part in the initial trial. They will be provided with compatible smartphones equipped with a special app developed in cooperation with Sharp.

Following the spring 2028 rollout, JR East plans to expand the technology to conventional railway and Shinkansen stations across its entire network, with the goal of introducing the walk-through system at every station that currently has automatic ticket gates, estimated to be around 550 stations, by the end of March 2032.

▼ This video shows how a wide range of commuters can benefit from the new gates.

The company says it’s looking even further ahead, with plans to introduce a GPS-based smartphone ticket gate system, provisionally named Smartphone Ticket Gates, in the mid-2030s. This would allow passengers to enter and exit stations using their smartphones’ location information, potentially removing the need for physical ticket gates altogether at JR East stations.

These new developments are all part of JR East’s wider “Suica Renaissance” initiative, which aims to expand Suica from a transport and small-payment system into a more comprehensive “everyday lifestyle service”. For a city where millions of people travel by train on a daily basis, the renaissance really does look set to make the commute even more seamless and stress-free for passengers.

title: Tokyo’s Akihabara planning crack-down on maid cafe promotional tactics
description: The otaku district is looking to fine and publish the names of violators of anti-kyakuhiki ordinances. Tokyo’s Akihabara neighborhood is famous for three things: anime, video games, and maid cafes. That third element, though, might be becoming less conspicuous soon, at least in terms of streetside presence, as the district is looking to crack down […]
content:
The otaku district is looking to fine and publish the names of violators of anti-kyakuhiki ordinances.

Tokyo’s Akihabara neighborhood is famous for three things: anime, video games, and maid cafes. That third element, though, might be becoming less conspicuous soon, at least in terms of streetside presence, as the district is looking to crack down on unauthorized maid cafe kyakuhiki promotions.

Kyakuhiki translates literally as “customer pulling,” and refers to the practice of barkers out on the street calling out to passersby to try to entice them to come to their eating/drinking establishment. Kyakuhiki is most commonly associated with izakaya (Japanese-style pubs), host/hostess clubs, and bars, but it’s also been a popular tactic for what Japan calls “concept cafes.” Not to be confused with themed cafes that serve up things like Final Fantasy Chocobo drinks or Kirby burgers, concept cafes are places that offer food, drink, and companionship, usually with a bit of costumed roleplaying from the staff, with maid cafes being by far the most prolific example.

It’s not at all uncommon to see maids doing kyakuhiki in Akihabara, either on the street right in front of their cafes or around the block from them. However, Tokyo’s Chiyoda Ward, of which Akihabara is a part, banned on-the-street kyakuhiki all the way back in 2014. Repeated reminders have failed to force compliance, though, and in 2025, the ward received nearly three dozen complaints about kyakuhiki staff being aggressively insistent or grabbing or otherwise touching people on the street.

After more than a decade of letting these violations slide, the ward has drafted a revised ordinance that would make kyakuhiki a finable offense. Under the new rules, both the employee performing the kyakuhiki activities and the owner of the business would be subject to a fine of 50,000 yen (US$315) and have their names publicly disclosed.

There is some leeway built into the new system, as the first two violations would only result in warnings. However, for owners operating multiple businesses the number of violations would be cumulative, so that if, for instance, after racking up three infractions for one maid cafe and being fined, the owner would then be fined for the very first violation related to another cafe they own.

The move comes as part of Japan’s recent reevaluation of lax regulations regarding misleading or manipulative behavior by bars, concept cafes, and host/hostess clubs. Last year, new ordinances were passed prohibiting the fraudulent exploitation of customers’ romantic feelings. There’s also been a surge in police complaints in Tokyo’s Shinjuku Ward regarding bar scams and rip-offs, with many of the complaints coming from foreign tourists, and with Akihabara also being a popular destination for visitors from oversees, no doubt there’s concern about damaging the neighborhood’s traveler-friendly reputation.

It’s worth noting that, in places where it’s allowed, kyakuhiki isn’t a tactic exclusively employed by places looking to scam customers. However, shady establishments tend to be particularly fond of it, and kyakuhiki being especially effective against customers who are weak-willed or easily susceptible to suggestion means there’s an increased chance of people who are drawn in by it then also being pressured to spend beyond their means once they’re inside the bar/cafe/club.

The draft for the new Chiyoda ordinance is expected to be formally introduced in February, and if passed would go into effect next spring.

Source: Yomiuri Shimbun via Kinisoku

title: 7-Eleven Japan taking a chance as it announces plans to sell Dr. Pepper nationwide
description: Just what the doctor ordered for fans of Japan’s most divisive soft drink. 7-Eleven Japan stocks a wide variety of products, but they’re pretty much all things that are popular with a large number of people in Japan. Things like rice balls with salmon flakes, cup ramen, bottled green tea, and canned coffee, that sort […]
content:
Just what the doctor ordered for fans of Japan’s most divisive soft drink.

7-Eleven Japan stocks a wide variety of products, but they’re pretty much all things that are popular with a large number of people in Japan. Things like rice balls with salmon flakes, cup ramen, bottled green tea, and canned coffee, that sort of stuff.

However, the chain is taking a chance with the newest addition to its lineup, a beverage that’s long been difficult to find in Japan because many retailers are intimidated by the prospect of trying to sell something so exotically unfamiliar and with such a divisive taste. And just what is this rarified elixir?

Dr. Pepper.

セブン‐イレブンでも遂に！全国で順次発売！

　 『ドクターペッパー 500ml』

｡o○ﾟ.｡o○ﾟ.｡o○ﾟ.｡o○ﾟ

長い歴史を誇る親しまれた炭酸飲料

飲んだことあるまだ飲んだことない
どちらの人もぜひ

みんなにも知らせようって思ったら➔リポスト pic.twitter.com/dvIBVbynZN

— セブン‐イレブン・ジャパン (@711SEJ) November 21, 2026

Carbonated soft drinks tend to be a tough sell in Japan to begin with. They’re often sweeter and heavier than what most Japanese consumers are looking for when they’re thirsty, and even Coca-Cola commands very little shelf space in stores and few slots within vending machines in Japan, compared to the numerous tea, coffee, and juice options. Dr. Pepper’s job gets even harder by nature of its complex spiced/herbal flavor. The flavor profile is much busier than that of Japan’s most popular drinks, and the most common complaint about Dr. Pepper among Japanese consumers is that it “tastes like medicine” (the “Dr.” part of the name probably doesn’t help in that regard either).

And yet, Dr. Pepper has managed to establish a small fanbase in Japan among those who can appreciate its unique charms. It’s not easy to satisfy cravings for such a niche beverage, though, which is why a while back the community created a sharable online map tracking every shop, restaurant, and vending machine in Japan where Dr. Pepper had been confirmed as being on sale. That map is going to be greatly expanding, as on November 21 7-Eleven Japan announced that it will begin selling Dr. Pepper at all of its branches nationwide, bringing cheers from online commenters such as:

“We can get Dr. Pepper at the convenience store now?!?”
“I wish this had happened sooner, but it’s still great news.”
“Filling the Dr. Pepper faithful with joy.”
“The intellectual beverage for the chosen elite is here.”
“I hope they start selling Diet Dr. Pepper too.”
“If you’ve tried Dr. Pepper and didn’t like it, please try it again, and don’t judge it until you’ve drunk two liters (68 ounces) of it.”

As the last comment illustrates, Dr. Pepper fans in Japan are ware that it can be an acquired taste, and even the drink’s Japanese marketing has acknowledged this, like this point-of-sale advertisement at a Japanese supermarket proclaiming “It becomes habit-forming after you drink it three times.”

近くのスーパーのキャンペーンで爆笑した pic.twitter.com/0VvkvC8qpG

— hodgstarr ホッジスター (@matth0dge) November 21, 2026

That might also explain why 7-Eleven is selling Dr. Pepper in 500-mililiter (16.9-ounce) bottles, but not 350-mililiter cans, since they could be betting on the larger serving size helping curious customers more easily get over initial unfamiliarity-triggered unpleasantness.

7-Eleven might also have been emboldened to start stocking Dr. Pepper by the success of Suntory’s Nope “guilty carbonated” soft drink, which boasts that it’s made from a whopping 99 fruit and spice flavors and is an unabashedly busy, heavy soda. Released last spring, Nope hasn’t won over everyone in Japan, but it’s sold well enough that retailers probably see new potential for similar drinks, such as Dr. Pepper.

Instead of a single release date, 7-Eleven Japan simply says that Dr. Pepper will be coming to its stores “in stages.” Some online commenters say it’s already arrived at their local branches, and now we’re wondering how long it’ll be until some of them try mixing it with melon soda like we did.

title: Godzilla and Fender reunite for some Telecasters made in monster heaven
description: Oh no, there goes Tokyo. The guitar artisans at Fender have been steadily pairing up with a range of Japanese pop-culture icons, including Evangelion, Hello Kitty, and Pokémon to name a few. Their 2025 collab Stratocaster with Godzilla in honor of the monster’s 70th anniversary was also a hit, so now, the big green smashing […]
content:
Oh no, there goes Tokyo.

The guitar artisans at Fender have been steadily pairing up with a range of Japanese pop-culture icons, including Evangelion, Hello Kitty, and Pokémon to name a few. Their 2025 collab Stratocaster with Godzilla in honor of the monster’s 70th anniversary was also a hit, so now, the big green smashing machine is back to return the favor.

Fender’s iconic Telecaster line of guitars saw its 75th anniversary this year, and just as the celebration is coming to an end, Godzilla has returned for more. It’s not really clear why guitars and Godzilla go so well together, but they do, and it really looks like all stops were pulled out to bring these two legends together in perfect harmony.

The first is the Made in Japan Godzilla Telecaster Black Paisley. Its black alder body has a classic paisley pattern on the front and back, with a late 20th-century Godzilla lovingly rendered on the front by artist Tom Neely in a way that seamlessly blends with the paisley pattern. Its black burst finish is so striking that these Telecasters have foregone pick guards and use dimmed black nickel hardware so the beauty can really shine through. Also, its C-shaped, 9.5-inch maple neck holds an Obsidian Ebony fretboard with the Godzilla logo and a city skyline just waiting to be thrashed. 

This merger of monster and rock doesn’t end with looks either. It has the same Custom Godzilla Humbucking pickup for that beefy kaiju heaviness that the previous Stratocaster had, and the master volume knob also has a push/push switch to activate a built-in distortion circuit meant to resemble Godzilla’s own roar.

The Made in Japan Godzilla Telecaster Black Paisley will begin taking preorders on 25 November, and can be purchased for 418,000 yen (US$2,600) in person at the Fender Flagship Store in Tokyo or online, where it can be shipped all over Japan, as well as the USA, Europe, and Australia. 

But this is just the beginning. A second collaboration guitar called the Fender Custom Shop Limited Edition Master Built Godzilla Telecaster is also in the works. Unfortunately, Fender has not released any images of this instrument yet, but according to the description, it will be crafted by master builder Andy Hicks with a two-piece alder body, quartersawn maple neck, and hand-wound pickup.

Tom Neely returns for the artwork and it sounds like he’ll be going all out on this model as well. According to the manufacturer’s description, on the front, Godzilla can be seen peacefully gazing towards Mt. Fuji, with waters reminiscent of Hokusai’s The Great Wave off Kanagawa in the background. On the backside, a more aggressive Godzilla will be bursting out of the ocean and letting loose a blast of atomic breath that stretches along the neck of the guitar. This will all be rendered in blacklight-reactive paint as well for a deeper feeling that is sure to make the atomic breath really pop.

This model will only be sold in Japan at the Fender Flagship Store or online, for a monstrous sum of 5,500,000 yen (US$34,500), which, interestingly, was the same price ESP’s Godzilla guitar sold for back in 2019. However, while ESP’s was a wildly original concept guitar that killed with looks, Fender’s version promises both an outstanding appearance and the craftsmanship to back up the sound as well.

title: Japan’s first-ever Pokémon Slowpoke donuts are here, and we’ve eaten them! [Photos]
description: Slowpoke kept us waiting for its Mister Donut debut, but was the wait worth it, or should we have bought two Pikachu donuts instead? Earlier this month, on November 4, Pikachu and Diglett arrived at Mister Donut for this year’s collaboration between the Pokémon franchise and Japan’s favorite donut chain. There are actually three Pokémon […]
content:
Slowpoke kept us waiting for its Mister Donut debut, but was the wait worth it, or should we have bought two Pikachu donuts instead?

Earlier this month, on November 4, Pikachu and Diglett arrived at Mister Donut for this year’s collaboration between the Pokémon franchise and Japan’s favorite donut chain. There are actually three Pokémon species that are getting turned into donuts this year, but the third was in no rush to coordinate schedules with the other two. Why?

Because Slowpoke always does things at his own pace.

Yes, this year marks Slowpoke’s Mister Donut debut, with the perpetually peacefully laidback Pocket Monster going on sale November 25. But even if Slowpoke wasn’t in any rush, I wanted to try this new treat ASAP, so I procured one on the first possible morning.

The Slowpoke Donut (or Yadon Donut, if you’re ordering it in Japanese) is priced at 345 yen (US$2.15) for takeout. That’s the same price as this year’s Fluffy Pikachu Donut, and since I didn’t want Slowpoke to feel lonely, I got one of those too.

Mister Donut and Pokémon have been partnering up for a couple of years now, and the art design for their collaborations is always adorable. The donuts came in this illustrated bag covered in cheerfully frolicking Pokémon, including the happiest-looking Psyduck I’ve ever seen.

▼ There’s a Pokémon 30th anniversary mark on the side too.

Honestly, if you’re a fan you could entertain yourself with the art for quite a while (most of the species are represented three times, making it kind of like a hidden-image game)…but the donuts are surprisingly fragrant, and their sweet aroma will waft out from the bag and compel you take them out.

Okay, Slowpoke, it’s time for your closeup!

Mister Donut wisely understands that fans will be snapping pictures of these donuts before they eat them, so they both come in little paper stands to make them easier to photograph.

Compared to the Pikachu donut, though, it’s a little hard to understand the form of the Slowpoke one, so let’s take it out and put it on a plate.

Now we can see that the unusual shape comes from bending a donut up in the middle of the ring, and giving the two parts different coverings.

The top half is dusted with strawberry milk sugar, and has chocolate eyes and ears filled with whipped cream. The other side has a white chocolate coating.

However, even after you’ve mentally grasped what the Slowpoke Donut is, it’s still kind of tricky to hold, and the unusual shape makes it hard to share with someone by taking alternate bites. I figured it’d be easier to take small, sensible bites if I separated the two parts…

…but doing so transformed Slowpoke into a creature with a terrifying, Predator-like maw.

▼ I think even the Pikachu donut was startled.

And things only got more shocking when it was cut into bite-sized pieces.

▼ Looking a little like Myaku-Myaku

However, there’s nothing fear-inducing about the flavor. The strawberry milk sugar is sweet without being cloying, and they didn’t go overboard on the tart notes for the fruit. The sugar provides a nice bit of crunch too. The whipped cream also focuses on sweetness more so than creaminess, with minimal oiliness.

Overall, the Slowpoke Donut is sweeter than the average Mister Donut offering, but since the chain’s donuts usually tend to be pretty mild in flavor, there’s room for them to be a little more impactful without overpowering your taste buds, and the Slowpoke donut turns out to be very tasty.

As for the Pikachu donut, it’s covered in little custard-flavored chocolate flakes, which also supplies some satisfyingly crunchy texture. Mister Donut bakes up Pikachu donuts every year, but the big change for the new iteration is that the red dots on his cheeks are now strawberry gummies.

These were honestly pretty hard, enough so that any of the soft donut you’re chewing in the same mouthful will be gone by the time you’re done chomping the gummies. They’re also tart enough to provide a short, sharp contrast to the sweet chocolate and cream, which you may or may not find as enjoyable as the more harmonious chocolate cheeks this donut used to have.

Whipped cream is the filling here too, and once again it’s refreshingly light in oiliness, letting the sweet notes play a bigger role and pairing nicely with the donut itself.

So Pikachu continues his success streak at Mister Donut, and Slowpoke turns out to have been waiting for. They’ll both only be available for a limited but unspecified time, though, so consider this your official excuse to eat multiple donuts in one day.

title: Taunting police by shouting “Shaolin Temple!” a growing trend among Japanese youth
description: Patience, grasshoppers. I long ago have come to accept that part of getting old means not understanding what the kids are into these days. I like to think I’m still hip by appreciating the whimsical chaos of something like Italian brain rot, but with each passing day, young people seem to find new ways to […]
content:
Patience, grasshoppers.

I long ago have come to accept that part of getting old means not understanding what the kids are into these days. I like to think I’m still hip by appreciating the whimsical chaos of something like Italian brain rot, but with each passing day, young people seem to find new ways to baffle me.

And I think today is the day I should finally start wearing suspenders and taking a vested interest in my digestion, because I have no idea what these kids are into. It’s being called the Shaolin Temple (“Shorinji” in Japanese) craze, and despite its name, it has seemingly nothing to do with warrior monks, Kung Fu, Wu Tang Clan, or the Japanese martial art Shorinji Kempo.

The core concept of Shaolin Temple, also known as Shaolin Temple Racing, is annoying police officers. In Japan, there are a network of police outposts called “koban” that serve as places you can go to turn in lost items, report crimes, or seek refuge if someone is after you. They’re often manned by around two officers at a time.

These huts also serve as prime targets for Shaolin Temple kids. The standard prank is similar to ding-dong-ditch, in that the kids will open the door to the Koban, scream “Shaolin Temple!” and then run away giggling. Some even go as far as jumping on the koban’s counter or prank calling the emergency hotline, 110, to shout the name of a temple at them. In every case, the stunts, ranging from annoying to criminal, are recorded on video and shared on social media.

▼ A news report showing some clips of Shaolin Temple incidents

According to reports, students from elementary school to high school have been detained or arrested for Shaolin Temple activities in the western prefectures of Osaka, Hyogo, Hiroshima, and Toyama, though it may only be a matter of time before the fad spreads further.

▼ Although not common in their area yet, a few days ago, the Tokyo Metropolitan Police took pre-emptive action and issued a warning that barging into a koban and shouting “Shaolin Temple” constitutes unlawful entry and is punishable by up to three years in a correctional facility or a 100,000 yen (US$630) fine.

【警視庁少年事件課からの重大なお知らせ】
「少林寺レーシング」と呼ばれる事案について
本当に警察を必要としている人の対処が遅れます。
悪ふざけでは済まされません。
警察は厳正に対処します。 pic.twitter.com/oo7iJVf82I

— 警視庁生活安全部 (@MPD_yokushi) November 20, 2026

No one is really sure why the kids are shouting “Shaolin Temple” of all things. Even kids who got caught and questioned by police can’t explain it, though it seems very likely the charm lies in the absurdity of it all. Many comments online, however, saw very little charm in the acts themselves and felt that social media and kids don’t mix.

“It’s the sense of unifying with peers and the thrill of doing something forbidden. Even if Shaolin Temple fades away, that spirit will remain.”
“The police should post videos of the punishments that come about in the Shaolin Temple aftermaths. That might help curb this trend.”
“Kids have been playing poli-oni [‘police onigoko’ or ‘police tag,’ hitting a police car to make it chase you] for over a decade now, but we can’t have police distracted when they’re needed for serious problems.”
“It just goes to show that the way to get popular on social media is to cater to the mentality of a 10-year-old.”
“They have no idea how lame that looks.”
“We should follow Australia’s example and ban social media for kids.”
“I’m feeling second-hand embarrassment just watching it.”
“I won’t stand for them dragging Shaolin’s name through the mud.”

It does seem like we’re due for another Kung Fu reboot, perhaps this time in the wild west of Japan. Shaolin monk Kwai Chang Caine narrowly escapes assassination in China and finds himself in Kansai, only to learn that his temple’s name is being used as a mere prank. He travels from town to town, teaching youngsters the true way of Shaolin and solving mysteries, with a guest appearance by William Shatner.

As for reality, I just hope kids can come to their senses and have fun the way we did before social media, by wearing beards made of bees and putting ferrets down our pants.

title: Noodle’s 24: Unstaffed make-your-own instant ramen stand is Harajuku’s newest hidden gem
description: How to eat cheap and try new ramen varieties at this “Self Noodle Shop” in Tokyo.  If you’re looking to discover the latest trends in Tokyo, Harajuku needs to be at the top of your list. Not only is it a famous hub for teenagers and cosplayers with their finger on the pulse for all […]
content:
How to eat cheap and try new ramen varieties at this “Self Noodle Shop” in Tokyo. 

If you’re looking to discover the latest trends in Tokyo, Harajuku needs to be at the top of your list. Not only is it a famous hub for teenagers and cosplayers with their finger on the pulse for all things kawaii, it’s also an exciting destination for anyone on the hunt for new food discoveries, as our reporter Mr Sato found when he stumbled across a new store in the area just the other day.

Called Noodle’s 24, this new joint is an unstaffed instant ramen shop where customers can pick out a pack of noodles, add toppings and prepare it all themselves. Originally hailing from South Korea, Noodle’s 24 is all about convenience – it even bills itself as a “ramen convenience store” – and it currently has two branches in Tokyo, one in Harajuku, which opened on 22 October, and one in Asakusa, which opened on 31 October.

▼ With no staff on site, everything is self-service, from payment and cooking through to clean-up afterwards.

▼ Inside, you’ll find shelves filled with packets of Japanese and Korean instant noodles.

The Japanese selection includes familiar favourites like Sapporo Ichiban Shio Ramen, Sapporo Ichiban Miso Ramen, Demae Iccho and Maruchan Seimen. All of these are priced at 500 yen (US$3.25).

The Korean selection contains 13 varieties, including the popular Shin Ramyun, with prices ranging from 500 to 600 yen.

While the noodle selection is impressive, so to are the toppings, as there’s an entire refrigerator stocked full of them. Priced between 100 and 200 yen, some of the options include green onions, corn, kimchi and pork back fat, so you can truly customise your ramen to your liking.

To place an order, simply use the tablet terminal near the entrance to select the products you’d like to purchase. There’s no need to scan barcodes, so be careful not to accidentally select the wrong items.

When Mr Sato finished making his selections and was ready to pay, a screen appeared asking him to enter the name he’d like to be called. He figured this was so his name could be called out when the order was ready, but that never happened so he’s not entirely sure why it was necessary.

▼ さとう = “Sato”

▼ Payment is cashless only, with various QR code payment services, credit cards and electronic money accepted.

After completing his payment, it was time to get cooking. Mr Sato chose something called Sari Gomtang, which had been described on the menu as “a Korean classic”. Looking at the cooking instructions on the back of the packet, he couldn’t understand the Korean writing, but as it was instant ramen, he decided to simply pour the powdered soup over the noodles, as he normally would.

After placing the noodles in the special cooking container, he sprinkled the soup powder over them, and then placed the container on the cooking machine and pressed the button marked “Ramen”.

▼ All that was left to do after that was simply wait for the machine to do its thing.

Though it might look like the machine simply dispenses hot water, that’s not all it does, as the flat surface is actually an induction heating unit, which helps to heat the noodles. Though Mr Sato initially wondered how the heating element would work with a paper container, it turns out that the base of the bowl is lined with aluminium, allowing heat to be transferred to the noodles inside.

▼ A very clever process.

Mr Sato barely had time to marvel at the machine before his noodles were done. He was so enamoured by the process that he even forgot to pause the machine and loosen the noodles while they were cooking, as recommended, but as these were instant noodles, which are hard to stuff up, he figured no harm was done.

▼ Another misstep was adding green onions as a topping for 100 yen, because the ramen already contained freeze-dried green onions in the packet.

As a lover of green onions, Mr Sato didn’t mind having extra, and when he took a slurp he was pleased to find that the noodles were pleasantly chewy, with a lovely texture. The beef bone broth had plenty of flavour and a satisfying depth of umami, giving the dish a distinctly Korean taste.

The noodles were hot and hearty, and Mr Sato particularly loved slurping them up inside the store, as it reminded him of the old “auto parlors” that used to exist along national highways in Japan in the ‘70s. These 24-hour rest stops were filled with arcade games and vending machines that served drinks and hot meals like ramen, making them particularly popular with long-haul truck drivers. Mr Sato would also stop by to use them in his hometown of Shimane when he owned a car and had late-night cravings for noodles.

He recalled one particularly cold winter, when he’d woken up in the middle of the night and couldn’t get back to sleep, so he drove over to the auto parlor and had himself a bowl of noodles. The store was completely deserted, with nothing but the background noise of the arcade games keeping him company as he slurped away. It was lonely, but somehow comforting and warm, and he remembered how those noodles tasted so good. Looking back, that was a real moment of luxury, and it was one he thought he would never experience ever again.

Though it wasn’t exactly the same, eating ramen at Noodle’s 24 brought him right back to that night with its auto parlor vibes. As a little hideaway where you can escape the hustle and bustle of the surrounding streets, this noodle joint is like an auto parlor right in the heart of Harajuku, and as they’re now pretty much non-existent in the way they used to be, any place that recreates the feel of an auto parlor is a great place to be.

title: This bento boxed lunch we got at a Japanese supermarket felt like a scam, but maybe it’s not
description: Can we find it in our hearts and stomachs to forgive this deceptive-looking bento? There’s a type of boxed lunch in Japan called the makunouchi bento, which is a boxed lunch with…well, pretty much whatever the person making it wants to put in there. Makunouchi doesn’t refer to any specific dish or ingredient. It actually […]
content:
Can we find it in our hearts and stomachs to forgive this deceptive-looking bento?

There’s a type of boxed lunch in Japan called the makunouchi bento, which is a boxed lunch with…well, pretty much whatever the person making it wants to put in there. Makunouchi doesn’t refer to any specific dish or ingredient. It actually just means, roughly, “behind the curtain,” and it originally referred to the boxed lunches eaten by theater workers during the Edo period, which consisted of white rice and whatever assorted small side dishes could be cooked or procured in and around the theater. Eventually, makunouchi bento became popular with audiences too, and then the general public, and now you can find them for sale even if you’re nowhere near the stage, including at just about any Japanese supermarket.

Now, buying a boxed lunch with a name that basically just means “rice and stuff” might seem like a huge risk, but the way that bento contents are arranged makes it easy to see what kind of sides you’re getting just by looking at it. For example, the makunouchi bento our Japanese-language reporter Yayoi Saginomiya recently picked up at budget-friendly supermarket chain Seiyu had rice sprinkled with black sesame seeds, nikudango (meatballs), kinpira gobo (stewed burdock root and carrot), tamagoyaki (a Japanese-style omelet), half a potato croquette, and benishoga (pickled ginger). Then, at the center of it all, was a slice of grilled salmon.

The salmon is definitely meant to be the star of the show here. Not only does Seiyu label this boxed lunch as a Coho/Silver Salmon Makunouchi Bento, the lid has a sticker on it proudly boasting that the slice of fish is flame-grilled before going into the box.

After arriving back home, Yayoi sat down, removed the lid, and got ready to dig in. Naturally, the first thing she wanted to try was that salmon, but as she angled her chopsticks toward it she couldn’t help noticing, now that she was looking looking at it from this perspective…

…that it was really thin.

And we mean really, really thin.

It couldn’t have been more than 5 millimeters (0.2 inches) in thickness. It was so thin that even one of Yayoi’s chopsticks, at the thicker end, had more girth.

At this point, Yayoi couldn’t help feeling ripped off, and we were having flashbacks to the convenience store “paper tiger sandwich” scandal that hit a while back. Granted, at 538 yen (US$3.40) this is a pretty inexpensive bento by today’s market conditions, but still, that’s a laughably thin cut of fish, and Yayoi can’t ever remember seeing grilled salmon sliced this thin before.

OK, so this bento is pitifully lacking in its quantity of salmon, but what about its quality?

Actually, Yayoi has got no complaints at all on that front. Compared to other types of salmon, coho salmon tends to have more fat, making it moist and tender. Those qualities were definitely present here, and the extent to which the fish had been grilled was pretty much perfect.

All of the other side dishes were excellent as well. The meatballs had just the right texture, neither tough nor mushy. The kinpira gobo was expertly seasoned, with the sweet, soy sauce notes of its broth pleasing the palate, as did the stimulatingly sweet tamagoyaki. The croquette had gotten a little limp as it had cooled off, but its flavor hadn’t suffered at all, and even the ginger worked great as a little sharp accent.

Again, there’s no getting around how thin and meager the cut of salmon is. After eating it, though, Yayoi came to the conclusion that, with costs going up, if a bento maker is going to try to keep their prices the same, she’d rather they keep the quality high, even if that means smaller portions, as opposed to maintaining the same size of all the dishes by switching to cheaper, poorer-tasting ingredients.

Still, Seiyu could stand to be a little more upfront about this, and odds are they’re not the only ones putting their bento components in the box in ways that make it hard to gauge their full size, so we’d recommend taking a close look from various angles if you really want to be sure of how big a lunch your boxed lunch is going to be.

title: Wild Pikachu tree appears in Japan! [Video]
description: Niigata town suddenly realizes part of its forests can do super-effective Pokémon cosplay. content:
Niigata town suddenly realizes part of its forests can do super-effective Pokémon cosplay.

You don’t have to be a catch-‘em-all completionist to see the appeal of the setting of the Pokémon games and anime. The idea that you could head out into the countryside and suddenly encounter something as cute and cool as a wild Pikachu is enough to get anyone excited.

Of course, such whimsical adventures don’t happen in the real world, right? Well, maybe they do, if you happen to be in Niigata Prefecture right now, where this recently appeared.

In a sleepy part of the town of Nagaoka, just a little off Niigata Prefectural Road 171 and a bit west of the Shibumigawa River, there’s a gingko tree that looks almost exactly like Pikachu. Though the tree itself isn’t new, it wasn’t until a few days ago that it started getting attention, as its leaves, now in their bright-yellow fall color, make the resemblance to the Pokémon mascot especially striking. As the only gingko tree in that part of the foothills, the silhouette really stands out, and if you’re fan of the franchise, it’s hard to see it as anything other than Pikachu.

Reactions from online commenters have included:

“It’s a wild Pikachu!”
“This isn’t even like ‘Yeah, now that you mention it…’ That’s totally Pikachu.”
“No way to not see that as Pikachu.”
“Do gingko trees dream of electric mice?”
“No throwing Poké Balls at the tree, everybody.”
“I feel like if this had happened 200 years ago, people would have said ‘There’s a demon in the tree’ or ‘This is an evil omen.’ I’m glad to be living in the present day.”
“Does this mean we’re going to see Pikachu here in the fall next year too?”
“I hope it evolves into Raichu.”

Unlike with Japan’s rice paddy art, this doesn’t appear to have been a planned, man-made art project. At the very least, no one’s come forward claiming to have been behind it, so for now it appears to simply be a genuinely cool coincidence. This sort of diagonally split top is an unusual feature for a gingko tree, but Google Streetview shows that the tree has been in that shape since at least August of this year, when the leaves were still green and no one had realized it was getting ready to cosplay as Pikachu.

If you do decide to head to this part of Nagaoka to check out Mother Nature’s Pokémon fan art project, though, remember that this is a residential neighborhood, so make sure to be respectful to the locals, stay off of private property, and not leave any trash behind. And if you’re looking for even more Pokémon in Niigata, they’ve got some special Magikarp too.

title: New Fuji Tram system is in development to help curb crowds, lessen environmental impact of cars
description: The tram route will connect the base of Mt. Fuji with the Yoshida Trail’s 5th Station as well as the under-construction Chuo Shinkansen maglev line. Yamanashi Prefecture unveiled plans on November 18 for a new public transportation system dubbed the Fuji Tram, with its name confirmed to be changed in the future. The tram will […]
content:
The tram route will connect the base of Mt. Fuji with the Yoshida Trail’s 5th Station as well as the under-construction Chuo Shinkansen maglev line.

Yamanashi Prefecture unveiled plans on November 18 for a new public transportation system dubbed the Fuji Tram, with its name confirmed to be changed in the future. The tram will take over the Fujikyu bus route currently in place along the Fuji Subaru Line toll road from the base of Mt. Fuji, where a new station is to be built (most likely on the west side of the Fujisan Parking lot) to the Yoshida Trail 5th Station, which is the most popular starting place for climbers. After the tram begins operations, private vehicles, buses, and taxis will no longer be allowed to use the road per Japan’s Road Traffic Act.

▼ This promotional video for the Fuji Tram also details plans to connect its new station with other regional tourism hotspots, including the Linear Chuo Shinkansen maglev line that’s currently under construction.

The adoption of the tram system is not meant to curb anyone’s fun but is a measure aimed at controlling the number of visitors and reducing the environmental impact of vehicles on Japan’s highest mountain. Yamanashi Prefecture previously imposed new daily climber restrictions and fees that went into effect last year, but concerns of overtourism still remain. The Fuji Tram plans are slated to restrict the number of visitors to the 5th Station to 2.3 million people annually, which is roughly on par with the number of visitors in 2012 before Mt. Fuji became a UNESCO World Heritage Site the following year. When selecting this limit, the government also took measures to avoid having the drop in visitors result in a negative impact on local economies.

Regarding the tram’s production, three different environmentally conscious plans are currently being considered: a Chinese-manufactured hydrogen and electric vehicle, as well as two different European-manufactured electric vehicles. All plans involve a vehicle with linked cars and rubber tires, though the former would be able to run in two directions while the latter only in a single direction. Total estimates for the construction and implementation costs are 77.3 billion to 96.5 billion yen (US$486.6 million to $607.5 million) depending on which plan is adopted, with the European electric vehicles costing on the lower end and the Chinese hydrogen and electric vehicle on the higher end. The project as a whole is expected to be funded by the third sector or Private a Finance Initiative (PFI) model.

▼ Capacity is expected to be 120 people per vehicle.

While there’s no current estimate for the start of operations, the Fuji Tram is expected to take 52-67 minutes from the new base station to the 5th Station, with vehicles running every 6-15 minutes (7-8 minutes on average). Round-trip passenger fare will be within 10,000 yen per person.

With the number of off-season climbers on Mt. Fuji facing increased scrutiny in Japan, hopefully the new Fuji Tram system will provide a more convenient and eco-friendly way for visitors to access the hiking trails during the mountain’s official climbing season as well.

title: After years of catering to foreign tourists, Osaka’s Kuromon Market wants locals to come back
description: It’s been a long time since many Osaka residents did their shopping in “Osaka’s kitchen.” Kuromon Market, or Kuromon Ichiba in Japanese, is a collection of roughly 150 shops along a 600-meter (1,969-foot) covered shopping arcade in Osaka’s Minami neighborhood. The market traces its history back to some 200 years ago, having started in the […]
content:
It’s been a long time since many Osaka residents did their shopping in “Osaka’s kitchen.”

Kuromon Market, or Kuromon Ichiba in Japanese, is a collection of roughly 150 shops along a 600-meter (1,969-foot) covered shopping arcade in Osaka’s Minami neighborhood. The market traces its history back to some 200 years ago, having started in the Edo period, and it’s sometimes been referred to as “Osaka’s kitchen.”

That nickname isn’t particularly accurate anymore, as in recent years Kuromon’s shops have shifted heavily towards catering to foreign travelers looking for photogenic street food instead of Osaka residents shopping for groceries. Now, though, Kuromon is looking to win back locals’ favor as tourist numbers start to dip.

Kuromon started out as a place where locals would buy basics such as fish, vegetables, tofu, and mochi. As time went on, some shops evolved into a sort of hybrid operation that sold both ingredients and prepared foods, and as more tourists started coming to the market for sightseeing, those prepared foods started shifting from everyday staples to more luxurious, flashy-looking, or simply inflated-price street foods, prices that local shoppers would balk at, but that travelers, who’d come to the market for special-occasion entertainment rather than errands, could more happily swallow.

This trend accelerated as overseas travelers started to outnumber locals at the market by a wide margin. With foreign tourists’ wallets stuffed with cash thanks to the weak yen, many of Kuromon’s merchants went all in on appealing to them, further pricing out locals to the point where many of them now see the market first and foremost as a tourist attraction/trap.

▼ Even the discounted 5,800 yen (US$36.50) is a ridiculous price for such a small tempura assortment, especially if you’re eating it in a casual market and not a fancy restaurant.

錦市場の次は、大阪の黒門市場にも来ていただきたいコケ https://t.co/SzOd6oSVvr pic.twitter.com/8PZjuTej3I

— ぽんタブ │ NIPPON-BASHI SHOP HEADLINE │ 大阪・日本橋 (@dendentown) November 7, 2026

The problem for Kuromon, though, is that Osaka isn’t attracting quite as many tourists these days. Though overall inbound tourist traffic to Japan remains high, there’s been a significant dip in the number of visitors from China, a demographic that’s traditionally made up an especially big proportion of Osaka’s foreign tourism. So with Kuromon seeing fewer foreign tourist customers these days, the market is now trying to woo back locals.

The efforts to do so are a joint project between the Kuromon Market Promotional Association, Osaka Metropolitan University, Kyoto Iken (a medical and health care specialty school), and the Kinki Newspaper Insert Advertising Association. Part of the plan involves leveraging students’ social media savvy, having teams of the teens and 20-somethings find shops and products in the market and showcasing them in posts to introduce “the Kuromon Market that Osaka residents don’t know about,” and the market started its own official Instagram account this past October.

▼ Kuromon Market’s official mascot character, Mon-chan, is an anthropomorphic kuromon (black gate).

View this post on Instagram

On the other end of the technological spectrum, Kuromon Market also recently printed 60,000 insert advertisements to be tucked into local newspapers. The market is also holding its first-ever Black Friday sale this year, running from November 18 to 28 (Japanese businesses have basically adapted Black Friday to just indicate “November sale”).

However, convincing locals to come back to the market is something that’s easier said than done. While some not unanimously negative, online reactions to some of Kuromon’s attempts show that there’s still some resentment towards the market for the foreign-tourist focus it’s had for the past several years.

“What, they’re going to have students tell each other to come drop 5,000-yen (US$31) for a basic lunch?”
“What a joke. Their food is way too expensive for Japanese locals. Good luck with selling it to foreign tourists.”
“That’s what you get for throwing away your local customers and just trying to profit off inbound tourists.”
“A while back, I was curious to see how badly Kuromon Market rips people off, so I went to take a look around…The prices were so ridiculous that it was actually kind of entertaining to see them, but I didn’t buy anything.”
“I remember them complaining about not having enough customers during the pandemic and pleading for locals to come…Then when the pandemic ended [and tourism opened up again] the prices went right back up.”
“They got themselves into this mess. Let them cry about it all they want.”
“They really gotta stop that habit of trying to cozy up to locals to help them out as soon as things start to go bad.”

Again, that’s not to say that everyone has written off Kuromon for good, and a number of online reactions to posts about the Black Friday sale have been from Japanese people saying they’re interested in paying the place a visit for the first time in a while. Still, there are clearly a lot of people whose image of the market has changed enough that they’ve lost all interest in it.

It’s worth keeping in mind that, for the entity of the two centuries that Kuromon Market has been around, its shops have always been businesses, and adapting to current economic conditions has long been one of the best ways for businesses to financially succeed. As Kuromon started getting more foreign tourists with more money to spend and an appetite for premium-priced products, it’s understandable that shops would want to give them what they want and make bigger profits for themselves. This eventually became a sort of self-propelling cycle: as more shops started offering more expensive foods, that in turn drew more tourists, so even fewer locals came to the market, so the focus on catering to tourists got even stronger.

Now, though, Kuromon is trying to figure out what to do when tourist demand contracts. The extra promotional efforts are all well and good, but a big question is whether the market is going to readjust back to more sensibly priced items, or if it’s going to try to find big-spending locals to replace the foreign tourists. The latter might prove difficult, seeing as how many Japanese households are having to tighten their budgets as consumer prices rise.

Kuromon probably won’t be the only place in Japan that’s going to have to deal with this sort of situation either. Kyoto’s Nishiki Market has similarly become extremely tourist-oriented in recent years, and certain touristy parts of Tokyo also have a reputation for restaurant prices that produce a laugh and “No thanks” from locals. It still remains to be seen whether Japan’s inbound tourism boom is a permanent change or something that’s going to cool off or be replaced by the next trendy travel hotspot, so it’s probably in businesses’ best interest to not alienate local customers while chasing after all that tourist yen.

As part of a collaboration with Final Fantasy and Dragon Quest, Chocobo and Slime, the video game franchises’ respective mascot monsters, are hanging out in […]
content:
It’s time for the mascots of Final Fantasy and Dragon Quest to make their Cosmo Clock debuts.

The city of Yokohama is hosting some very special guests this holiday season. As part of a collaboration with Final Fantasy and Dragon Quest, Chocobo and Slime, the video game franchises’ respective mascot monsters, are hanging out in the Minato Mirai harbor district, where special FF and DQ Christmas trees have gone up, and where fans can grab a bite to eat at a limited-time themed cafe.

The decorations include some huge Slime and Chocobo balloons, but the two stars are now getting even bigger. When you have a guest, it’s only appropriate that you give them the nicest seat in the house, and Minato Mirai does something similar for visiting characters by giving them a spot on the Cosmo Clock, the neighborhood’s massive, 100-meter (328-foot) diameter Ferris wheel. title: Tomb festival in Osaka holds qualifying tyrannosaurus race and ancient clay sculpture chase
description: Ready to unpack all that? Monday 23 November is a public holiday in Japan, creating a long weekend this year, which is always a good time to hold a major event. In Osaka, that meant it was time once again for Kofun Fest Hanicotto, a regional festival celebrating ancient Japanese graves at Imajozuka Kofun Park. […]
content:
Ready to unpack all that?

Monday 23 November is a public holiday in Japan, creating a long weekend this year, which is always a good time to hold a major event. In Osaka, that meant it was time once again for Kofun Fest Hanicotto, a regional festival celebrating ancient Japanese graves at Imajozuka Kofun Park.

A kofun is an ancient tomb typically reserved for royalty. Since Osaka was an ancient capital of Japan and adjacent to other historical capitals like Nara and Kyoto, the city is dotted with quite a few of them, easily spotted in aerial photos due to their large sizes and distinctive, keyhole-like shapes.

▼ Here are a few of them.

As for “Hanicotto,” that is a combination of the words “haniwa” and the Japanese pronunciation of “mascot.” Players of Animal Crossing ought to be somewhat familiar with the ancient clay sculptures known as haniwa that resemble scared or confused cactuses. These figures were buried with the deceased in kofun to help protect them in the afterlife.

▼ Kofun Fest Hanicotto was also the venue for HaniCon 2026.

With all this talk of fifth-century Japanese culture, you’re probably wondering, “This is all well and good, but why aren’t there any dinosaurs here, too?” Well, I was just getting to that.

For a few years now, Kofun Fest Hanicotto has also been the host of the West Japan qualifying round of the Tyranno Fest national Tyrannosaurus rex race. This is the only qualifying race of its kind on this side of Japan and promises to bring the very best in men, women, and children who run around while wearing a big T-Rex costume.

The first and second-place male and female racers, as well as one wildcard entrant who wins the MIP (Most Impressive Participant) award, advance to Tyranno Fest Vol. 3 on 20 March, 2027 at Funabashi Racecourse in Chiba Prefecture.

The Kofun Fest Hanicotto races are prestigious events in this dignified spot. At Tyranno Fest Vol. 1, the women’s champion came from Kofun Fest Hanicotto, as did the men’s champ in Tyranno Fest Vol. 2. This grand prix of T-Rex racing is a gate-style sprint, in which the dinos start behind closed gates like racehorses, presumably because it looks really funny.

These qualifying rounds, however, are standard time trial races, combined with Kofun Fest Hanicotto’s signature Haniwa Capture Race, where the Tyrannosaurus Rexes have to also pick up haniwa statues on the ground, and probably fall down a lot in the process.

The main sponsor of this event is none other than Zenpo-Koenfu, a grave operator that has made headlines for their award-winning modern Takeda-style kofun tombs. The centerpiece of these is a stylish reimagining of the ancient burial grounds that lies atop Mt. Ikoma, overlooking nearly all of Osaka Prefecture in a picturesque park designed by the firm of noted architect Tadao Ando. It won the Kansai Region Grave Grand Prix for both its layout and as a convenient, cost-effective alternative to traditional family graves.

All in all, it’s a great time to learn about Japanese burial methods old and new, while also watching people dressed as dinosaurs wobble around for a bit. Although this year’s event is behind us now, it’s sure to return next year, bigger and more ancient than ever.
