title: Conveyor belt sushi chain Sushiro quadruples its prices for first branch in America
description: Enthusiastic diners show up for Sushiro’s opening in New York, fans in Japan experience sushi sticker shock. Last week, Japanese conveyor belt sushi chain Sushiro made its American debut. The chain’s first-ever branch on U.S. soil, located in New York, welcomed its first customers on November 19 with long lines of diners waiting to get […]
content:
Enthusiastic diners show up for Sushiro’s opening in New York, fans in Japan experience sushi sticker shock.

Last week, Japanese conveyor belt sushi chain Sushiro made its American debut. The chain’s first-ever branch on U.S. soil, located in New York, welcomed its first customers on November 19 with long lines of diners waiting to get in.

It’s not just Manhattanites’ whose attention has been grabbed, though, as people in Sushiro’s home country of Japan have been shocked at the prices being charged by the New York branch.

As you can see in the above video, Sushiro wasn’t hurting for customers on its opening day, with some people arriving hours before its 11 a.m. opening in order to be some of the first seated. Diners seemed very happy with the quality of the food too in the on-site interviews that have been posted.

Sushiro has brought over several aspects of the chain’s dining experience from Japan, including large tough-screen panels for placing orders and a no-tipping policy, which is the norm in Japan but a rarity for restaurants in America. That doesn’t meant that Sushiro is positioning itself as a budget restaurant in the States, though, as its prices start from US$5 a plate for standard types of sushi like maguro (tuna), and more expensive ingredients, like otoro (extra-fatty tuna) cost US$10. Those prices convert to about 800 and 1,600 yen. Meanwhile, if you go to a Sushiro in Japan…

…you can get a plate of maguro for 180 yen, and the vast majority of its sushi can be had for 210 yen or less. In other words, Sushiro is charging about four times as much in the U.S. as it does in Japan.

Is that too much? That’s actually a pretty complicated question. Right off the bat, the yen is extremely weak versus the U.S. dollar right now, so it’s natural for prices to be higher in the U.S. In addition, Sushiro’s first American branch is in Manhattan, one of the most expensive neighborhoods in one of the most expensive cities in the country.

If we figure an average-sized sushi meal is going to be somewhere within the range of 5 to 10 plates, that’s make a meal at Sushiro New York cost US$25-US$50. That’s not an eye-popping price for a meal out in Americas these days, and even if we convert that to 4,000-8,000 yen, that’s not a shocking amount of money for one person to spend on a restaurant sushi meal in Japan. It is, however, a startling amount of money for someone in Japan to spend on a Sushiro meal.

In the Japanese restaurant industry, you could say that Sushiro occupies a space similar to the one In-N-Out Burger has in America. For its segment and price point, it has a reputation for excellent quality, and so it has a lot of loyal fans, enough that you’ll often find long lines during the lunch or dinner rush, or when a new branch opens and marks the chain’s first arrival in a neighborhood. However, no one in Japan considers Sushiro to be high-end dining. Sure, the food is tasty, but the décor, ambiance, and overall vibe isn’t particularly luxurious or otherwise rarified, so quadrupling the price really messes with its perception as being good quality at a good price, leading to online reactions in Japan about the New York opening such as:

“800 yen a plate? Man, America is expensive…”
“Way too steep, No way I’m eating Sushiro at that price!”
“I can’t even laugh at how expensive that is.”
“It’s nice that they say ‘no tips,’ but it’s crazy to [quadruple] the price compared to Japan.”
“I can get a whole lunch for 800 yen.”
“People are seriously lining up down the street and paying those prices to ear at a basic chain restaurant?”
“I don’t think it’s gonna last.”

Ultimately, though, all that really matters is whether diners in New York are OK with those prices, and that’s something we won’t know for a while. Again, figuring a price of US$25-$US$40 for a meal, Sushiro isn’t an exorbitantly expensive option by American restaurant prices, but it’s also not a particularly cheap one either, especially for customers with big appetites who’ll need more than 10 plates to feel full. Because of that, Sushiro really is going to have to convince customers that it’s a restaurant worth paying a bit of a price premium for, and to that end, the interior does look a little fancier than what you’d see at a Sushiro branch. The New York branch also has private rooms for groups of diners, though these also are for more expensive fixed-price course meals.

▼ One of the Sushiro New York private dining rooms can be seen in the video here.

On the other hand, there’s a risk that the conveyor belt delivery system and giant touch panel used for ordering, once the novelty wears off, might seem more gimmicky than high-tech classy, and no matter how nice the restaurant’s interior is, being located right next door to a McDonald’s could also impact how special a visit to Sushiro feels, at least in terms of being someplace at which to splurge on an expensive, or at least not-cheap, meal.

For now, though, it looks like Sushiro is off to a good start in the States, and can now focus on finding ways to keep customers coming back.
